content.thinking:
I'm working through the postmortem's symptom section: latency rose with the slowest requests taking much longer, errors stayed flat, and the slow pages look like account pages. The series is p99 overall, and the code path points at render_spend_summary calling typical_spend_per_item, though that hasn't been run yet.

I'm now drafting the causal chain, starting with the symptom: the slowest requests took much longer while the error rate stayed within its normal range. Next I'm checking whether the flag changes at 14:15 and 14:16 tie the slowdown to the typical-purchase path, and whether any deploy or earlier change could account for it instead.

Next I'm checking the deploy and flag history for anything else that could explain the slowdown, and noting that the flag evaluations switched on from the minute the latency rose.

I'm now weighing the performance cost in the flag-on path: with the flag enabled, account page requests run a per-shopper typical-spend calculation, and its cost grows with how long each shopper's purchase history is.

Now I'm settling the root cause: the typical-spend helper in typical_spend.py finds the middle price by repeatedly scanning for and removing the minimum, so its cost grows much faster than the length of the purchase history, and shoppers with long histories are the ones who waited.

I'm settling how to phrase the root cause without naming a complexity class or any specific size: the helper keeps removing the smallest price to reach the middle, with a full pass over the list each time, so the work grows far faster than the purchase history itself. I'm also drafting a plain-words version of the cause, that switching on the feature sent shoppers' pages through a typical-spend calculation that likely does more work the longer a shopper's purchase history is, which is why those shoppers waited longer.

I'm settling on how to word the next stretch of the postmortem: the flag switch was an admin action, and I'm keeping the slowest-requests description free of specifics. For the remaining risk, I'm noting that turning the typical-purchase feature back on before a fix ships could slow the slowest requests again in the same way, and I'm moving on to the contributing factors, starting with how the flag was switched on for all production traffic at once.

I'm settling the contributing factors: the flag was switched on by an admin for all production traffic at once, with evaluations going from all off to all on within about a minute, and no staged rollout or automatic latency rollback showed up. A staged rollout would have limited exposure to a fraction of shoppers, and a latency guard would have turned the flag off sooner, so I'm proposing flag changes go through a staged rollout with a latency check that can switch them off. I'm also noting that no performance test with large purchase histories ran before the change shipped, so I'm proposing performance tests with large-input cases for code behind flags before enabling.

I'm checking that the contributing factor about paging doesn't belong among the contributing factors, since paging wouldn't have shortened the outage, so it goes under what went wrong with an action item to route the alert to on-call instead.

I'm turning to the action items now: a staged rollout for flag changes on io-shop to cover the all-at-once switch-on, an automatic guard that turns a just-enabled flag back off when tail latency rises, a test with long purchase histories before any flag goes live, and routing the HighLatency alert to on-call paging. I'm also starting the went-well list, noting that the Investigator tied the onset to the flag switch and the Mitigation Agent turned the flag off.

I'm noting the first steps for the postmortem: the Mitigation Agent confirmed the service was back below incident level after the flag was turned off, and the Code-Fix Agent proposed a draft fix PR. The only thing that went wrong is that nobody was paged, since no on-call incident was linked to the alert. There's nothing else to record under what went wrong, and I'm leaving the got-lucky list empty.

I'm noting the assumptions the postmortem rests on: that the slow requests came from shoppers with long purchase histories is inferred from Code-Fix's reading of the code, not measured per shopper, and the latency series is the highest p99 across replicas. I'm also checking the alert label and the start of the timeline before moving on to the next step.

I'm checking the flag evaluations: from the onset onward every logged evaluation came back on, where before every one had been off. I'm also ruling out deploys, since none came back, and ruling out other flag changes, since the only one recorded in the hour before was the admin's switch.

I'm checking the root-cause wording against the contributing factors: the flag was on, so requests ran the typical-purchase path, which is why the slow shoppers waited. I'm deciding that a long-history test would likely have caught the cost before the flag went live, and I'm confirming the labels I'll use in the timeline don't need any extra figures.

I'm settling on how to phrase the latency figures for the postmortem, keeping the wording on the tail latency and the slowest requests rather than any specific percentile.

action_items.item: Roll out io-shop feature flag changes to a small share of traffic first, rather than to every request at once.
Add an automatic guard that switches a recently changed io-shop flag back off when tail request latency rises after the change.
Require a cost-bounding test with large inputs, such as long purchase histories, for code behind a feature flag before that flag can be switched on in production.
Route the io-shop HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' slowest requests took much longer to load. The alert fired on the slowest tail of request durations across the service's replicas, and the Investigator placed the start at the onset. Failed requests did not rise: the account page error rate stayed within its usual range and peaked before the onset.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release: the search of production change events covering the day before the onset returned only this flag change, and no deploys.
Any other flag change: the flag provider's history for the hour before showed only this one change by anyone but Argus.

causal_chain.step: Requests began running the code path behind typical-purchase-feature. Admin switched the flag on at {P1.1}. Before that, every flag evaluation logged came back off. In the minute of the switch the evaluations were mixed, and from the onset on, every evaluation logged came back on.

With the flag on, the account page's spend summary calls a typical-spend calculation whose work, by Code-Fix's reading, grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so shoppers with long histories waited much longer.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new shop feature sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend that likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages for shoppers with long purchase histories became very slow.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off for every evaluation to on for every evaluation within about a minute. No staged rollout to a small share of shoppers was seen, and no automatic guard that turns a just-changed flag off when latency rises was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged rollout would have exposed only a few shoppers to the slow path, and a latency guard could have turned the flag off without waiting for the alert and an agent's action.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test or check of how the flagged code path performs with long purchase histories was seen before the flag was switched on in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test with a long purchase history would likely have shown the slow calculation before the flag was turned on, so the slow path would not have reached shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read metrics, change events, the service register and logs, and formed a single candidate tying the slowdown to the flag switch.
The Mitigation Agent turned typical-purchase-feature off, an action that can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service, found it no longer at the incident's level, and confirmed the action.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #573 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was brought in while the incident ran.

input.root_cause: With typical-purchase-feature on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). That function finds the middle price by removing the smallest remaining price over and over until it reaches the middle, and each min and each remove is a full pass over the list. Its work therefore grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became very slow while requests for most shoppers stayed fast.
input.still_at_risk: If typical-purchase-feature is switched back on before a fix is in place, the slowest shop requests could slow down again in the same way.
input.symptom: The slowest shop page loads slowed sharply for some shoppers
